1:
After heaping question upon question through the long survey of the created world, the LORD pauses, and into Job's silence presses one demand more. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the whole weight of the two preceding chapters gathered into this single application: having shown Job, by his manifest ignorance of the works of nature, what an incompetent judge he was of the methods and designs of Providence, God clenches the nail with one further question. He supposes that God paused awhile, as Elihu had done, to give Job time to say what he had to say or to weigh what had been said; but Job remained silent in his confusion, and so God here put him upon replying. This word, Henry notes, is not said to be spoken out of the whirlwind, as before, and some think God uttered it in a still small voice, which wrought upon Job more than the whirlwind did, as it had upon Elijah at Horeb in 1 Kings 19:12-13. Though Job had said nothing, God is still said to answer him, for he knows men's thoughts and can return a suitable answer even to their silence.

The reformed John Gill reads the pause the same way: the LORD, having discoursed largely of his works to reconcile Job's mind to his providence, stopped and made a little space that Job might answer if he thought fit; but finding him entirely silent, God began again.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke stands apart, less on the sense than on the setting. "Answered," he insists, does not refer to anything Job had said or asked; and he thinks it very likely that this whole piece, from the first verse to the fourteenth, was originally the ending of the poem. Following Mr. Heath, he argues that since Job 42:7 shows Jehovah to be the last speaker, the fourteen verses now opening the chapter belong rather after Job 42:6, where they would furnish the grand and solemn catastrophe of the poem, the skins of parchment composing the ancient roll having, he supposes, changed their places. Gill and Henry simply take the verse where it stands. So a real difference opens at the very threshold of the chapter: whether the challenge here begins God's second address, read in its received place, or is a displaced fragment of the poem's true close, sewn in out of order. However the leaves of the roll are arranged, the witnesses agree on the thrust of the moment, that a God who has just paraded the wonders of his hand now turns and waits for the answer of the man who had dared to arraign him.
2:
The challenge itself is put as a question no honest man can answer but one way: shall the creature who wrangles with his Maker set up to teach him? The reformed John Gill presses the absurdity of it. He that takes upon him to dispute with God, to object and reply, to bring a charge and litigate a point, ought to be capable of instructing him; but could Job, or any other, instruct the God of knowledge, the all-wise and only-wise, who himself gives man wisdom and teaches him knowledge? What folly, Gill exclaims, to pretend to instruct him! He who will contend with the Almighty should be above all instruction from God or man, a teacher and not one taught; and since he plainly is not, the very posture of contention convicts him of presumption.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the Hebrew and find in it a climax. The question with the particle stands to the earlier challenge in the relation of a step upward: Job had not merely contended with God, which is wrong whatever the ground, but had gone so far as to lose sight of the divine justice in the government of the world, and, rather than give up his own righteousness, had come near to doubting God's. The censurer, the fault-finder who sets God right as though he knew everything better, is now bidden answer the questions put to him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps it short and sharp: let the man who has made so free with God and his government answer to what he has now heard.

The other grammatical-historical voice, Charles Ellicott, would render the line rather, "Can the contending with the Almighty instruct him?" and unfolds the drift of the whole speech behind it. God is about to show Job his inability to govern the world and administer judgment among men from his acknowledged inability to govern the more formidable animals of the brute creation: if he cannot restrain them, how shall he tread down the wicked in their place, or hold them in check, or deliver himself from the hand of God? Ellicott adds that it might make these verses more effective to transpose Job's coming resolve after Job 42:6 and regard it as the very climax of the poem, as some have done; yet he judges this neither necessary nor supported by any external evidence, and is content to read the words where they lie. The witnesses do not divide over the force of the demand: it is a question asked in disdain, and its only fitting answer is the silence of submission.
3:
The narrative turns on a single, quiet clause, and the witnesses mark how much it carries. Where through all the friends' speeches Job had been quick to reply, here, at the voice of God, he answers only under compulsion. The reformed John Gill catches the reluctance in the very brevity: finding that he was obliged to answer, Job did so, but with some reluctance, a man who had longed to reason with the Almighty now scarcely able to frame a word before him.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note the shift of address that the verse records. Job answers not Zophar, nor Bildad, nor any of the men who had come to instruct him, but Jehovah; and this, they observe, is the point at which the speech of God has in some measure attained the end assigned to it, so that the challenge could now be taken up again. It is the same movement they trace through the whole of the second discourse: God does not demand blind subjection but free submission; he does not extort an acknowledgement of his greatness, but effects it by persuasion, so that the answer, when it comes, is drawn out and not compelled by terror.

The verse is a hinge, and its very plainness is eloquent. Through two and thirty chapters Job had been the ready speaker, pressing his cause, demanding a hearing, sure that if he could but come to God's seat he would order his cause before him and fill his mouth with arguments. Now the hearing he had craved is granted, God has spoken, and the man who had so much to say stands almost mute. That he answers at all is significant, for silence pressed too far becomes sullenness, and God had bidden him reply; but that he answers so briefly, and with such reluctance, shows how wholly the ground has shifted beneath him. The friends he had answered as an equal; the LORD he can only answer as a suppliant. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the turn from the wrangling of the debate to this halting reply is the first visible sign that the divine speech has done its work, and that the next words from Job's lips will be not the vindication he had prepared but the confession of a man undone. The eager pleader of the earlier chapters has become the hesitant respondent, and the change of tone is itself the beginning of his repentance, the quiet before the great self-abasement that the following verse will pour out.
4:
"Behold, I am vile" — with these three words Job lays down the whole apparatus of his defence, and the witnesses gather to weigh how deep the confession runs. The reformed John Gill turns the word over in several senses. It may be rendered "light," and refer to his words and arguments, which he had thought weighty but now saw to have no force; or to his works and the integrity of his life, imagined to be of great importance but, weighed in the balances of justice, found wanting; or to his original meanness and distance from God, being dust and ashes and nothing in comparison of him, so that the Septuagint reads "I am nothing"; or, rather, to the vileness and sinfulness of his nature, now laid bare, having broken forth in unbecoming expressions concerning God and his providence. The nature of man, Gill says, is exceeding vile in soul and body, and of this an enlightened man is convinced and will acknowledge.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the confession bare and personal: "I acknowledge my inward defilement. I cannot answer thee. I cannot excuse myself, and I must be dumb before thee."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the whole descent of the penitent. Now Job came to himself and began to melt into godly sorrow; when his friends reasoned with him he did not yield, but the voice of the LORD is powerful, and when the Spirit of truth comes he shall convince. Job owns himself an offender with nothing to say in his own justification; sin debases us, and penitents abase themselves, are ashamed, yea confounded. Job now vilifies himself as much as ever he had justified and magnified himself, for repentance changes men's opinion of themselves. He had been too bold in demanding a conference with God, thinking he could make his part good with him; but now, convinced of his error, he owns himself utterly unable to stand before God or to produce anything worth his notice, the veriest dunghill-worm that ever crawled upon God's ground, as he had once confessed himself the work of God's hands in Job 10:9. In answer to the demand that he reply, he lays his hand upon his mouth, keeping it as with a bridle to suppress all passionate thoughts; for, as the wise man teaches in Proverbs 30:32, if thou hast thought evil, lay thy hand upon thy mouth and let it go no further. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that those truly sensible of their own vileness dare not justify themselves before God, but, in token of their shame, fall silent under his hand.
5:
Job seals his silence with a solemn measuring of his fault: once he has spoken, twice, and now he will speak no more. The reformed John Gill takes the words as the settling of a resolve. Some, he notes, refer this to the confession Job has just made of his vileness, that being all he had to say and all the answer he would give; and he records that Jarchi supposes Job to have respect to earlier words of his, retracted now that God has spoken. Either way, having once let his passion vent itself, Job will not answer, will not stand to what he has said, nor say it again.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the doubled phrase, "once, yea twice," as the idiom for what has been done repeatedly, and hear in the resolve the true note of submission: Job will proceed no further, laying down the cause he had so hotly pressed. And they use the moment to mark the temper of the whole second discourse. This second time also Jehovah speaks to Job, not in wrath but in the profound condescension of his majesty, to deliver his servant from dark imaginings and bring him to free and joyous knowledge; for God is much more forbearing and compassionate than men. Observe the friends, they say, those sticklers for their own orthodoxy, how they rave against Job: how much better is it to fall into the hands of the living God than into the hands of man, for God is truth and love, while men have at one time love without truth, at another truth without love.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verse as the utter collapse of Job's self-defence: "I shall attempt to justify myself no longer; I have spoken repeatedly, and am confounded at my want of respect for my Maker, and at the high thoughts I have entertained of my own righteousness. All is impurity in the presence of thy Majesty." Yet Clarke, consistent with his theory of the poem's order, would read this resolve to speak no more as belonging properly to the very climax after Job 42:6, since as the text now stands Job does speak again. The witnesses do not divide over the sense. They agree that Job here binds himself to silence, not in sullenness but in shame, a man who has weighed his own words and found them too many, and who will now let the LORD have the last as well as the first word.
6:
The submission just made was real, but the witnesses see that it was not yet full, and so the LORD speaks a second time out of the storm. The reformed John Gill weighs whether the whirlwind had ceased or continued. Some think it fell silent while God spoke the opening challenge, which emboldened Job to answer; but Gill judges rather that it went on, and now increased. For comfort does not always follow immediately on first convictions: Job, though humbled, was not yet humbled enough, and God will have a fuller confession from him. It was not sufficient to say he was vile; he must declare his sorrow for sin, his abhorrence of himself for it, and his repentance; and though he had said he would answer no more, God will make him say more, and therefore continued the whirlwind, having more to say and a further proof of his power to give.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the renewed address as a law of the spiritual life. Job was brought low, but not low enough, and therefore God proceeds to reason with him in the same manner as before, as he had first challenged him in Job 38:3. Those who duly receive what they have heard from God, and profit by it, shall hear more from him; and those truly convinced of sin and penitent for it have yet need to be more thoroughly convinced and more deeply humbled. Henry draws the pastoral warning out at length: those under conviction, who have their sins set in order before their eyes and their hearts broken for them, must learn from this instance not to catch at comfort too soon. It will be everlasting when it comes, and therefore it is necessary that we be prepared for it by deep humiliation, that the wound be searched to the bottom and not skinned over, and that we make no more haste out of our convictions than good speed. When our hearts begin to melt and relent within us, let those considerations be dwelt upon which will help to make a thorough and effectual thaw.

That the second speech, like the first, issues from the whirlwind is itself a mercy in Keil's reading, carried forward from the previous verse: God speaks out of the storm not to crush but to persuade, that his servant might come to a knowledge that is free and glad. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the renewed voice from the whirlwind is no fresh outburst of anger but the pressing of an unfinished work, God returning to a wound half-searched, resolved to bring his servant not merely to say he is vile but to loathe the sin and rest wholly in the grace that is about to raise him.
7:
The second speech opens as the first had done, with a summons to Job to brace himself and stand up to be questioned. The reformed John Gill notes only the bare demand, that Job gird up his loins like a man, God about to ask and Job to answer. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the challenge in its rising order. The question that follows stands to the earlier one as a climax: Job had not merely contended with God, which is in itself wrong, but had gone so far as to lose sight of the divine justice in the government of the world, and, rather than surrender his own righteousness, so far as to doubt God's. In the governing of the world God shows his arm and raises his voice of thunder; can Job, who seems to imagine he could govern better, do the like? The gird-up-thy-loins, they observe, is the language of a combatant called to the field, and God meets Job's craving for a hearing by granting it on his own terms.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks the repetition and makes of it an argument for his theory of the text. "Gird up thy loins" he refers back to the opening of the first speech in Job 38:3, and some think, he says, that this verse and the one before it have been repeated here from that place, and that several of the words there, here, and later have been repeated in after times to connect some false gatherings of the sheets of parchment on which the end of the poem was originally written. So even the challenge itself becomes, for Clarke, a seam where the displaced leaves of the roll were stitched together.

Whatever be thought of the order of the leaves, the witnesses agree on the sense of the summons. It is the challenge that every proud heart must come to at last, either by its repentance or by its ruin, and thus low must every mountain and hill be brought. God does not answer Job's complaints with a soft word but with a call to stand up and make good his cause if he can, knowing that the very attempt will teach the man his measure. The command to play the man is, in the mouth of God, an act of grace disguised as a challenge: it invites Job to the contest precisely that he may learn, past all doubting, that he is no match for his Maker, and so be brought willingly to the submission that terror alone could never produce.
8:
"Wilt thou also disannul my judgment?" — the question cuts to the root of Job's error, and the witnesses feel its edge. The reformed John Gill takes the "judgment" to be the decrees and purposes of God concerning his dealings with men, and particularly their afflictions, framed with the highest wisdom and the strictest justice and never to be frustrated; or the sentence gone out of his mouth, which cannot be altered; or the execution of it, which cannot be hindered. To set up one's own judgment against the Lord's is, as much as in a man lies, to disannul it; whereas God is a God of judgment, and his judgment is according to truth, and will take place, let men say what they please.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the pair, "Wilt thou altogether annul my right, condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous?" and read the second speech as putting Job's whole complaint to the test: he is bidden, for once, to put on the robes of the King of kings, to send forth his wrath over pride and evil-doing for their complete removal, and see whether he can. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on the deeper fault the question exposes: rather than submit to be thought in the wrong, will Job condemn God's conduct in order to justify his own? Some men, Clarke observes, will never acknowledge themselves in the wrong; "God may err, but we cannot" seems their impious maxim, for there are three words most difficult to pronounce in any language, "I am wrong."

The other grammatical-historical voice, Charles Ellicott, compares the charge with Job's own earlier words, where he had cried out of wrong and complained that God had taken away his right, and unfolds the argument the whole speech is mounting. God is about to prove Job's inability to govern the world and administer judgment from his inability to govern the more formidable of the beasts: if he cannot restrain them, how shall he tread down the wicked in their place; and if he cannot hold the wicked in check, how shall he protect himself, much less deliver himself from the hand of God? The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the lesson. Many of Job's complaints had too much of this tendency, as if he would bring a writ of error to reverse the judgment of God as unjust; but God's judgment cannot be disannulled, for it is according to truth, and our duty is to condemn ourselves that God may be righteous, as David does in Psalms 51:4. Those are very proud, and very ignorant of God and of themselves, who to clear themselves will condemn him. The witnesses do not divide: to make God unjust that one may seem just is the last and worst turn of self-defence, and the very thing this question is framed to shame.
9:
From the justice of God the challenge passes to his power: has Job an arm like God's, or can he thunder with such a voice? The reformed John Gill measures the distance the question opens. God's power is infinite, almighty, and uncontrollable, and therefore there is no contending with him; the same arm on which good men lean and by which they are supported and saved is the arm that can crush like a moth all who strive against him. The mere naming of it settles the case: a creature with no such arm has no business disputing the acts of him who has.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke feels the cumulative force of the whole passage. Every word from here to the end of the strophe, he says, has a wonderful tendency to humble the soul; and it is no wonder that at the conclusion of these sayings Job fell in the dust confounded and ascribed righteousness to his Maker. The question is not one link in an argument but the first blow of a series meant to lay a proud man low.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the two things the verse denies to Job, that he can neither fight it out with God nor talk it out with him. He could never carry his cause by force of arms, for all the forces he could raise against the Almighty would be but as briers and thorns before a consuming fire, as in Isaiah 27:4. The power of creatures, even of angels, is derived, limited, and dependent; the power of God is original, independent, and unlimited: he can do everything without us, we can do nothing without him, and therefore we have not an arm like God. Nor could Job carry his cause by noise and big words, as men sometimes do; he cannot thunder with a voice like God's, whose voice will soon drown his, and one of whose thunders will overrule all his whispers. God's creating voice is called his thunder in Psalms 104:7, and the voice with which he discomfits his enemies in 1 Samuel 2:10; the wrath of a king may sometimes roar like a lion, but can never pretend to imitate God's thunder. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the two clauses interrogative, not optative: in the government of the world God shows his arm and raises his voice of thunder, and the question is whether Job, who talks as though he could rule better, can do the same. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the challenge is unanswerable, and meant to be, drawing Job to own that neither in strength nor in majesty of speech is he anything before the God he had presumed to correct.
10:
If Job would enter the lists with God, let him first put on the robes for it; the challenge shifts from power to splendour, bidding him deck himself with majesty and array himself in glory. The reformed John Gill hears God saying, in effect, deck thyself now with such excellent majesty as I am decked and clothed withal, a garment no creature can so much as counterfeit. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns it upon Job's presumption: act like God, seeing thou hast been assuming to thyself the perfections that belong to him alone; wear, if thou canst, the majesty thou hast dared to arraign.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as the opening of a mock-investiture. Job is for once to put on the robes of the King of kings, to wrap himself round with pomp and dignity and clothe himself in glory and majesty, and then, so arrayed, to send forth his wrath over pride and evil-doing for their complete removal. The irony is grave rather than cruel: God offers Job the very insignia of divine rule, knowing he cannot bear them, that the offer itself may show him the gulf between the creature who complains and the Creator who governs.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the comparison to its full length. If Job will vie with God and appear the more admirable, let him deck himself with majesty and excellency and array himself with glory and beauty, appearing in all the martial pomp and royal pageantry he has, making the best of everything that will set him off. But what is it all to the divine majesty and beauty, no more than the light of a glow-worm to that of the sun when he goes forth in his strength? God decks himself with such majesty as is the terror of devils and all the powers of darkness, and arrays himself with such glory as is the wonder of angels and of all the saints in light; David could dwell all his days in God's house to behold the beauty of the LORD. In comparison with this, what is all the majesty by which princes make themselves feared, and all the glory by which lovers make themselves beloved? If Job thinks, in contending with God, to carry the day by looking great and making a figure, he is quite mistaken, for the sun itself shall be ashamed and the moon confounded when God shines forth. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the challenge to robe himself in glory is one Job cannot meet, and that the very splendour he is bidden to assume is the measure of how far the disputant falls short of the God whose government he had presumed to judge.
11:
The robed pretender is now bidden do a king's proper work, to pour out his wrath and bring the proud low; and the witnesses hear in the command both an impossible demand and a revelation of God. The reformed John Gill paraphrases the summons as a challenge to Job's temper: work thyself up into a passion, at least seemingly, put on all the airs of a wrathful king on his throne, whose wrath is as the roaring of a lion and as messengers of death; pour out menaces plentifully, threatening what thou wilt do, and try whether by such means thou canst humble the spirit of a proud man. The point of the mockery is plain: the rage Job had been casting toward heaven would move no proud tyrant on earth, still less the God he flung it at.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse, "Let the overflowings of thy wrath pour forth, and behold all pride, and abase it," taking the word for wrath in its proper sense of oversteppings or overflowings, the flood of anger a king lets loose. In this, they note, one is directly reminded of the great judgment on pride that runs through the prophets, God alone being able to send such a flood where it belongs.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse a proof of Godhead. By this God proves himself to be God, that he resists the proud, sits judge upon them, and is able to bring them to ruin. Proud people are wicked people, Henry says, pride lying at the bottom of a great deal of the wickedness in the world, both toward God and toward man; and proud people will certainly be abased, for pride goes before destruction. If they bend not, they will break; if they humble not themselves by true repentance, God will humble them to their everlasting confusion. He can do it, and does it easily, bringing the proud low with a look, overwhelming them with shame and fear and utter ruin by one angry glance, as by a gracious look he revives the hearts of the contrite. And here the challenge doubles back on Job, who had been passionately quarrelling with God's providence, ready to charge him with mal-administration for suffering tyrants to prosper: let Job try his hand first upon the proud, and he will soon see how little they value the rage of his wrath, and how absurd it was to think that God should be moved by it. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that only God can flood the earth with a wrath that lays pride in the dust, and that the very grandeur of the office proves how far it lies beyond the reach of the man who had presumed to sit in judgment on its exercise.
12:
The demand of the previous verse is pressed home and made more searching: Job is to look on every proud man, bring him low, and tread down the wicked where they stand. The reformed John Gill dwells on that last phrase, "in their place," and finds in it the reach of the impossible task. The wicked are to be trodden down wherever they are found, though they pretend to have a place of their own and to have taken root in it; and yet even there they shall be trodden down, and all the wealth and power and interest to which their place entitles them will be no security. To abase the proud in the very seat of their strength is the work Job is challenged to attempt, and it is a work no arm but God's can do.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the sense forward from the flood of wrath just named: having poured out his anger, Job is to behold every one that is proud and humble him, and cast down the evil-doers in their place, as one who could dispose of the mighty at his word. The command is one link in a chain of demands, each requiring the very sovereignty over pride and power that belongs to God alone; and the naming of the wicked "in their place" measures the completeness of the rule that would be needed, a dominion reaching every proud man in his own stronghold.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as part of the cause God here puts upon a short issue: if Job can humble and abase proud tyrants as easily and effectually as God can, it shall be acknowledged that he has some colour to compete with his Maker. By this very thing God proves himself to be God, that he resists the proud and sits judge upon them; proud people will certainly be abased and brought low, for they that will not bend shall break. The wicked shall be trodden down in their place, Henry says, wherever they are found, their pretended rootedness no defence against the tread of divine justice. And the challenge is aimed straight at Job's complaint: he had murmured at the prosperity and power of oppressors, and was ready to charge God with mismanaging the world for suffering it; but he ought not to find fault except he could mend, and if God alone has power enough to bring the proud down, no doubt he has wisdom enough to know when and how to do it. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the treading-down of the wicked in their place is a divine prerogative, and that the demand lays bare how little the murmuring sufferer could do of what he had presumed to criticize God for delaying.
13:
The judgment on the proud is followed to its end, the grave: Job is bidden hide them all in the dust together and bind their faces in the secret place. The reformed John Gill takes the hiding in the dust of death or of the grave, that the proud might be seen no more where they had lorded it, given an inglorious burial like malefactors thrown together into a common pit, as when multitudes slain in battle are cast without order or decency into one wide grave. He notes too that the word may be rendered "alike," that they be treated all as one, no preference given to the great above the mean, the high and the low blended in a single ruin.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same levelling into the first clause, to blend the high and the low, the rich and the poor, in one common ruin, and so show that God is supreme and can do whatever he pleases. But the second clause he takes with a striking literalness, referring "bind their faces in secret" to the custom of preserving mummies: the whole body wrapped round with strong swathings of linen, the very head and face rolled about with filleting so that not one feature can be seen, not even the rise of the nose, and on the outside a human face painted, while the real face is emphatically bound in secret, those rollers never meant to be removed. So the proud, who gloried in their looks, are swaddled out of sight as the dead are.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the imagery of the verse to a solemn point. God will at last do the work effectually, not merely bringing the proud to the dust, from which they might hope to rise, but hiding them in it, like the proud Egyptian whom Moses slew and hid in the sand in Exodus 2:12, brought not only to death but to the grave, that pit out of which there is no return. They were proud of the figure they made, and shall be buried in oblivion, no more remembered than those hidden in the dust. They were linked in leagues to do mischief, and now are bound in bundles; they are treated as malefactors, whose faces were covered when they were condemned, or as dead men bound about the face in the grave. Thus complete, Henry says, will be the victory God gains at last over the proud sinners who set themselves against him. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the burying of the proud in the dust, faces bound out of sight, is a work of divine justice Job could never perform, and that the demand to perform it is meant to bring the complainer to own how far the government of the world lies beyond his hand.
14:
The long challenge closes with a promise Job can never claim: if he can do all this, then God himself will confess that his own right hand can save him. The reformed John Gill spells out the concession and its impossibility. Could Job abase the proud and hide them in the dust, God would own that his right hand could save him from all his enemies, temporal and spiritual, and that he stood in no need of help; but since he can do none of the things proposed to him, it cannot be admitted that his own hand can save him, and therefore he ought to submit quietly to God's sovereignty and be humbled under his mighty hand. No man's right hand, Gill adds, can save him from temporal evils, much less from spiritual ones, or with an everlasting salvation; only the arm of the LORD has wrought salvation, and his right hand alone supports and saves.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke makes the verse the crown of the whole speech and reads its condition as a manifest absurdity that teaches a gospel. When thou canst extend an arm like God, arm thyself with the lightning of heaven, deck thyself with the glory of the supreme majesty, dispense thy judgments over all the earth to abase the proud and tread down the wicked, and blend the high and low in the dust, then, and not till then, will I acknowledge that thy own right hand can save thee. In other words, Clarke says, salvation belongs to the LORD; no man can save his own soul by works of righteousness he has done or can do to all eternity, and without Jesus every human spirit must have perished everlastingly.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the challenge a rebuke of man's oldest ambition. It is the innate pride of man that he would be his own saviour, would have his own hands sufficient for him and be independent; but it is presumption to pretend it, for our own hands cannot save us by recommending us to God's grace, much less by rescuing us from his justice. Unless we could by our own power humble our enemies, we cannot by our own power save ourselves; yet if we could, God himself would confess it, for he never did nor will defraud any man of his just praise. Since we cannot, we must confess that our own hands cannot save us, and into his hand commit ourselves. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the promise is framed on a condition no creature can meet, and that its whole design is to drive Job, and every reader, from all trust in his own arm to the God whose right hand alone can save.
15:
"Behold now behemoth, which I made with thee; he eateth grass as an ox" — and with these words the speech turns from the abasing of the proud to the wonder of a single beast, over whose very name the witnesses fall to disputing. The reformed John Gill observes that the word is plural, signifying beasts, and may denote the chiefest and largest of them, whence it is commonly understood of the elephant, the Septuagint rendering it by the Greek word used for that animal; yet he reports that Bochart dissents from the received opinion and holds for the hippopotamus, or river horse, so called from its horse-like head, mane, and snout. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, weighing the same alternatives, confesses he sees no reason to depart from the ancient and most generally received opinion that it is the elephant, a creature of such vast stature and wonderful sagacity that among so many beasts already surveyed it could scarcely be passed over; the river horse and the bull he sets aside.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke breaks with both. Having carefully read all that Bochart, chief of the learned, has urged, he doubts whether either the elephant or the hippopotamus is meant, or whether any animal now in existence answers the description; with Mr. Good he supposes the creature extinct, and identifies it with the mammoth, whose recovered bones argue an animal twenty-five feet high, fitly called the chief of the ways of God. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott finds the identification a standing difficulty: the Hebrew is the natural plural of the word for domestic cattle, which might suggest that more than one animal is meant, the earlier verses fitting the elephant and the later the hippopotamus; he notes a Coptic word for water-ox that may lie concealed in the name, yet grants that the hippopotamus neither frequents mountains nor eats grass like an ox.

Against all these stands the latin-fathers reading of Gregory the Great, who takes Behemoth allegorically, not as any brute at all but as the ancient enemy described under that name: the proud become the more familiarly devoted to him the higher they swell with the successes of this life, feeding the hunger of this Behemoth with their thoughts without number as with the hay of the field. So the debate is fourfold, whether the beast be elephant, river horse, some extinct giant, or a figure of the devil himself. On the closing clause, "which I made with thee," the witnesses draw together: Ellicott hears God skilfully reminding Job that he shares a common origin with the beasts, a fellow-creature made to inhabit the world with him, and Henry that God made the beast on the same day as man, in Genesis 1:29 appointing herbs for the food of both, so that man and beast are jointly kept by Providence as fellow-commoners, as the psalmist owns in Psalms 36:6.
16:
The description of the beast begins with its seat of strength: its power is in its loins and its force in the muscles of its belly. The reformed John Gill grants that the strength of the elephant is well known, able to carry a tower and a company of armed men on its back; yet he adds, with a candour that runs through his whole comment on this passage, that what follows does not seem so well to agree with it, a first hint that the received identification may not answer at every point.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take the verse as the opening of the anatomy that runs on through the following lines, reading the strength in the loins and the force in the sinews of the belly as the frame of a creature built for sheer power, the giant of beasts whose very name, though plural in form, denotes the beast by eminence. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, faithful to his mammoth, refers the strength of the loins not to bulk merely but to agility: notwithstanding the creature's size, by the strength of its loins it could take vast springs and make astonishing bounds, a nimbleness he thinks fits neither the ponderous elephant nor the wallowing river horse.

The other grammatical-historical voice, Charles Ellicott, corrects the rendering of the second clause. Where the English speaks of the "navel" of the belly, the word means rather the sinews, or muscles, so that the force is lodged in the great cords of the creature's frame. It is a small point of philology, but of a piece with the running debate, for each witness reads the anatomy toward the animal he has already fixed upon. The verse itself does not name the beast; it only measures its might, laying the ground of the argument the whole passage presses, that a creature so mightily built is yet but a thing God made, and made with Job, so that the strength which no man could master is wholly at the disposal of the God who framed it. The witnesses do not finally divide over the sense of the words. They agree that the loins and the belly-sinews are named to set before Job an image of overmastering strength, and they part only in the application, Gill already doubting the elephant, Clarke pressing his leaping giant, Ellicott fixing the muscles where the older version had put the navel, each feeling after the identity of the creature through the strength the verse ascribes to it.
17:
The moving of the tail "like a cedar" is the first feature over which the witnesses openly break ranks upon the creature's identity. The reformed John Gill notes at once that the comparison cannot be for length or largeness, since the tails of both elephant and river horse are short; it must be for smoothness, roundness, thickness, and firmness, such as the river horse's tail has, like that of a hog or boar, which it turns and twists at pleasure. He records Aben Ezra's rendering "maketh to stand," stiff and firm like a cedar, and even the reading of Junius and the Targum, who refer the word not to the tail at all but to another extreme part of the body, Cicero remarking that the ancients were wont so to name it; the very obscurity of the line breeds a crowd of guesses. Gill notes too that one writer speaks of the horse of the Nile as having a scaly tail, though he seems to confound it with the sea horse, and that the elephant's tail, on Aristotle's report, is but small and out of all proportion to the bulk of its body, a further reason the comparison sits ill with that beast.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the same feature into a proof against the two usual candidates. "He moveth his tail like a cedar," he says, and therefore it was neither the elephant, whose tail is like a hog's, nor the hippopotamus, whose tail is but a foot long; and the second clause he translates, with Mr. Good, of the sinews of the haunches rather than the stones, as still more characteristic of an animal that must have excelled in leaping. The cedar-like tail becomes, in his hands, one more mark of the extinct and mighty creature he supposes.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott is briefest of all, correcting only the anatomy: the "sinews of his stones" are rather the sinews of his thighs. The exactness is characteristic, and it leaves the larger dispute untouched, for the question of what beast bends a tail like a cedar remains open. So the identity of Behemoth, raised at the naming of him, is pressed here at a single stubborn detail: Gill feeling after the river horse yet unsure, Clarke certain the tail rules out both elephant and hippopotamus and points to his leaping giant, Ellicott content to fix the word for the thighs and let the creature be. The witnesses do not resolve it. They agree only that the image is one of massive and controlled power, a tail wielded with the force of a great tree though it be no cedar in length, and they carry their unsettled question forward to the harder anatomy of the bones that follows, where the same division will appear again.
18:
The strength of the frame is now driven home by repetition: the bones are as strong pieces of brass, the bones like bars of iron, than which nothing is harder. The reformed John Gill hears the doubling as made for greater illustration and confirmation, the same thing said twice for emphasis; but he cannot let it pass without noting that it is not well applicable to the elephant, whose bones, as the anatomists show, are for the most part porous and spongy, light and rimous, save only its teeth, the ivory. The teeth of the river horse, he adds, are reckoned harder than ivory and wrought with greater difficulty, so hard that the ancients used them in place of it and that fire may be struck from them; and by this comparison too the balance, for Gill, tips away from the elephant.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the brass and iron of the bones toward his own creature, remarking that the tusk he had spoken of before is uncommonly hard, solid, and weighty for its size, the sort of bony strength a mammoth would show. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott offers a quieter emendation, rendering the "strong pieces" as perhaps tubes, so that the sense runs, his limbs are like bars of iron; the metaphor is not of solid rods but of the great hollow tubes of the creature's legs, strong as forged metal.

The verse adds no new debate but sharpens the old one, each witness reading the iron bones toward the beast he has chosen. What none of them doubts is the point the imagery serves. The bones of brass and bars of iron are set before Job as the last word in creaturely solidity, a frame that no force of man could bend or break; and yet, as the next verse will say, the God who forged that frame can bring his sword near it and unmake in a moment what he made. The witnesses do not divide over the plain sense. They agree that the piled-up figures of brass and iron are meant to overwhelm, to leave the hearer with an impression of invincible strength, precisely so that the reminder of the Maker's power over even this may fall with the greater weight. Gill's doubt about the elephant's spongy bones, Clarke's hard tusk, Ellicott's iron tubes, all serve the one design, to magnify a strength that only its Author could overmaster.
19:
"He is the chief of the ways of God" — the great title given the beast draws the witnesses back to their dispute, for each reads the pre-eminence toward his own creature. The reformed John Gill takes "chief" as either the beginning of God's works, which would fix the beast among the animals made on the fifth day, the river horse being of the water and so made before the elephant of the sixth; or as expressive of a superior excellency, in which case it must be limited to the creature's own kind, since man is the chief of all God's works. So he can call the river horse the chief of the aquatic and amphibious animals, for the bulk of its body, not unlike the elephant's, as the elephant is chief of the land beasts. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke seizes the title for his mammoth, "the largest, strongest, and swiftest quadruped that God has formed," a creature no power of man or beast could overcome, whom God alone could make and God alone unmake.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott judges the phrase more applicable to the elephant than the hippopotamus, considering the great intelligence and usefulness of the elephant, which set it above the brutes. On the obscure second clause he is fullest of all, laying out the renderings side by side. Some read, "He only that made him can bring his sword near unto him"; others, "He that made him hath furnished him with his sword"; others again, "He that would dress him as meat, let him come near him with his sword," a phrase marking the inequality of the contest; and Ellicott himself thinks a combination best, "Let his Maker, but no one else venture to, approach him with his sword."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, holding for the elephant, hears in the same clause the great use of the whole description. He that made the beast, notwithstanding its bulk and strength, can make his sword approach to it, can unmake it at pleasure and kill an elephant as easily as a worm or a fly; for he who has power to create with a word has power to destroy with a word, and may do what he will with his own. And Henry sees the beast made to represent the proud tyrants God had just challenged Job to abase, who think themselves as well fortified against his judgments as the elephant with his bones of brass and iron; but he that made the soul of man knows all the avenues to it, and can make the sword of justice, his wrath, approach it in the tenderest part. Woe, then, to him that strives with his Maker. The witnesses divide over the beast but not over the doctrine: whatever creature is the chief of God's ways, its Maker holds the sword over it, and man, its fellow-creature, has less cause still to contend with God.
20:
The mountains yielding the creature its food furnish another disputed sign, and the witnesses read it toward opposite animals. The reformed John Gill takes the mountains bringing forth food to mean the grass that grows on them, so much of it that only mountains can supply so vast a feeder; and he presses the marvel that a creature bred in a river should come out of it to seek its food on the heights. He supports this by the strange account of the northern morss, or sea-morss, much like the river horse, which climbs by its great teeth to the mountain-tops, feeds on the grass, and rolls itself down again into the sea, an exotic parallel he offers for the amphibious behemoth.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch turn from the beast to its shade, dwelling on the botany of the lines that follow. They read the verse as describing how harmless and, if unmolested, inoffensive the animal is where it grazes; and they identify the shade-tree named just after as the lote-tree, the wild jujube or Rhamnus, which likes hot and damp valleys and is found much on the shores of the Sea of Galilee, its small yellow fruit called dûm, the very tree whose shadow the wild creatures of the steppe are known to seek. The learning is poured out on the setting rather than the disputed name, fixing the scene in a real Eastern landscape of lote-tree and marsh.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes the mountains as decisive against the hippopotamus, which is seldom found far from the rivers where it lives; a creature fed on the mountains, where all the beasts of the field play about it and it makes a mock of them all, answering, he insists, to the mammoth and not at all to the river horse. So the same clause is claimed by both parties, Gill making the mountain-grazing an argument for the amphibious river horse that leaves the water to feed, Clarke making it an argument against the water-bound hippopotamus and for his land-ranging giant. The witnesses do not resolve the identity, and Gill's tale of the mountain-climbing morss stands out as the oddest of the proofs offered on either side. Yet beneath the dispute lies a shared and gentler note, caught by Keil: the beast at its grazing is peaceable, the field-beasts playing beside it without fear, an image of untroubled and God-given strength that harms nothing while it is left alone.
21:
The scene softens to the creature at rest, lying under the shady trees in the covert of the reed and the fen; and here the witnesses, briefly, find less to dispute and more to picture. The reformed John Gill gives the verse almost in its own words, the beast lying under the shade in the covert of the reed, a couch of green retirement for so vast a body. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke owns the limits of knowledge here: this verse and those about it refer to certain habits of the behemoth with which we are, and must be, unacquainted, a candid confession that the ancient poet describes what no modern eye has watched.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, weighing the resting-place, thinks the description on the whole more appropriate to the elephant than the hippopotamus, and turns aside to expose the reasoning that has swayed the critics. Their judgment, he says, has been biased by their preconceived notions about the circumstances under which the Book of Job was written; it is thought the author was more likely to have known the river horse of Egypt than the elephant of India. But elephants abound also in Africa, Ellicott points out, and may very well have been known to the writer of Job from that quarter, if the Indian is less likely, so that the argument from the poet's supposed horizon cuts less deeply than its users suppose.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, in his running view of the beast, sets its shady lodging against the dens of beasts of prey. The behemoth lodges under the shady trees, where it has free and open air to breathe, while lions, which live by prey, when they would repose must retire into a close and dark den, as the earlier chapter had shown in Job 38:40. Those who are a terror to others cannot but be sometimes a terror to themselves; but those will be easy who let others be easy about them, and the reeds and fens and willows of the brook, weak fortification though they are, suffice for the defence of a creature that dreads no harm because it designs none. The witnesses do not sharply divide. They agree that the picture is one of peaceable and unguarded strength, a mighty beast at rest among the marsh-grass, and they part only in the old undertone, Ellicott inclining to the elephant, Clarke confessing ignorance, Gill and Henry content to draw the quiet moral of a power that harms nothing and so has nothing to fear.
22:
The shade of the previous verse is doubled here, the lote-trees covering the beast with their shadow and the willows of the brook compassing it about; and the witnesses read the leafy covert once more toward their rival creatures. The reformed John Gill hesitates over the fitness of the image for the elephant, since, on the authority of Aelian and others, the elephant rarely lies down but sleeps standing, finding it troublesome to rise again, and is besides reckoned by some taller than the trees; whereas the lying down under the shade, and the willows of the brook that follow, seem to him to agree better with the river horse, a creature of the water's edge among the reeds and boughs.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks the same clause with his usual brevity, granting that "the willows of the brook compass him" would agree well enough with the hippopotamus, the one point at which the amphibious animal seems to fit the description without strain. It is a fair-minded concession from the champion of the mammoth, an admission that the marsh-side setting suits the river horse if anything does; and it is the more striking coming from a witness who at almost every other feature had pressed the case for his extinct and land-ranging giant, so that here, for once, he lets the willows of the brook speak for the creature of the water.

The verse, brief as the witnesses' comment on it, deepens the picture of untroubled repose the preceding lines began. The great beast is hidden in green shade, ringed round by the willows of the stream, a body of iron bone and mountain bulk laid down among the softest and slenderest of coverts. The very gentleness of the scene is part of the argument, for the strength the earlier verses piled up is here shown wholly at rest, harming nothing, sheltered by the trees God planted for it as surely as he framed its bones. The witnesses do not resolve the standing question of the creature's name; Gill leans, on the ground of the lying-down and the willows, toward the river horse, and Clarke allows the brookside willows to the hippopotamus, so that here, unusually, the two incline the same way. What both feel is the poet's design: to set before Job an image of vast power at peace in its appointed place, that the man who could neither make nor master such a creature might learn again how little cause he had to contend with the God who made it and gave it its couch among the reeds.
23:
"Behold, he drinketh up a river, and hasteth not" — the creature's vast and fearless thirst is the theme, and the witnesses weigh both the image and its rendering. The reformed John Gill grants that the elephant is a thirsty animal that drinks largely, the philosopher reporting it takes many measures at a draught; but to drink up a river seems to him too great an hyperbole, and so he prefers the reading, "let a river oppress him," bear ever so hard upon him, "he hasteth not" to escape it, is not frightened or troubled. This, he says, agrees with the river horse, which walks into the stream and proceeds with the greatest unconcern, now and then lifting its head above water to breathe, and can hold its breath long, whereas the elephant cannot wade beyond the reach of its trunk above the surface, and Livy tells of elephants seized with fear and trembling at being ferried over a river.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verse of a creature that no river can stop, comparing the fierce horse of the earlier chapter that "swalloweth the ground" in Job 39:24: the behemoth wades through all, stems every tide, and hurries not as one in danger. "He trusteth that he can draw up Jordan" means that even when the river overflows its banks it is no stoppage to him; though the whole impetuosity of its stream rush against his mouth, he is not afraid. Clarke commends Mr. Good's rendering, "If the stream rage, he revileth not; he is unmoved, though Jordan rush against his mouth," and from the mention of Jordan judges it probable that the behemoth once inhabited the marshes and woods of Palestine.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott settles the sense with a cleaner rendering: "Behold, if a river overflow, he trembleth not; he is confident, though Jordan swell up to his mouth." The naming of Jordan is proverbial for a strong, swelling stream, and the point is the creature's magnificent composure before a flood that would sweep other beasts away. The witnesses do not divide over that point. They agree that the verse paints an unshakable confidence, a strength so at ease with the raging water that the torrent breaking on its very mouth cannot move it; and they part only in the old way, Gill hearing in the calm wading the river horse, Clarke his Jordan-haunting giant, Ellicott content to fix the grammar and let the great beast stand unafraid in the flood.
24:
The description of the beast ends on the near-impossibility of taking him: he is to be caught, if at all, only by his eyes, and his nose pierces through the snares. The reformed John Gill reads the verse of the difficulty of the capture, whether of elephant or river horse: neither is to be taken openly but only by craft, and he tells how the elephant was trapped in pits dug and covered over, into which it was decoyed, and how the river horse likewise falls unawares into a pit hidden under reeds and sand. The creature's very wariness, taken "by his eyes," is part of the picture of a strength no open force can master.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it of the beast's contempt for restraint: he looks at the sweeping tide and defies it, and his nose pierces through snares, so that if fences of strong stakes be made to hold him, he tears them in pieces or breaks them with his nose. Were other parts of the description to answer, Clarke allows, this might well fit the elephant, the nose being the proboscis with which it can split trees; but he holds to his mammoth, ending the whole account with the judgment that the creature is some extinct giant, the chief of the ways of God, whose bones God's providence has preserved that later ages might admire the power that made it. Here too Clarke gathers up his long textual argument, that the fourteen opening verses of the chapter are dislocated: following Dr. Kennicott, he reasons that the description of these creatures is strangely interrupted at the head of the chapter and as strangely resumed at the naming of behemoth, and that a leaf of the roll, holding just those verses, was sewn in after Job 39:30 instead of after Job 42:6, so that, restored to its place, the poem would end grandly with the voice of Jehovah.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the disputed clause with care. Some, he notes, read it as a question, "Shall any take him with snares? while he is looking, shall any pierce through his nose?"; but the sense seems rather, "Let one take him by his eyes," that is, by allurements set before him, as elephants are taken, and "by means of snares one may pierce his nose," the Authorised Version being the less probable. The witnesses do not divide over the drift of the verse. They agree that it crowns the portrait with the creature's near-untakable strength, a beast to be caught only by stealth if at all, and part only where they have parted throughout, Gill between elephant and river horse, Clarke pressing his extinct giant and his transposed leaves, Ellicott fixing the grammar; and with this last unconquerable image the great description of Behemoth is brought to its close.
